blocks.text: ...in everyday routine
The “stand” procedure is suitable for all situations in which the dog is exposed to no distraction or to absolutely unproblematic distraction.
“Stand” is a good alternative to “sit” in all kinds of environmental conditions that make a “sit” inadvisable – such as unfavourable ground conditions, extreme weather conditions and the like.
“Stand” is also suitable for situations that require only a short halt, and for simple encounter situations.
Start, prerequisites and training frequency 📋
Start: From about the 5th month of age.
Training frequency: Daily in suitable situations – starting without distraction and, over time, under growing stimulus levels.
Execution and training environment 🌿
Ideally we train “stand” on the walk, initially on the leash, in a quiet, low-stimulus environment.
Later, as responsiveness grows, training may take place as appropriate to the situation under steadily increasing stimulus levels.
“Stand” is one of the calmest exercises in its introduction and execution – it takes a lot of patience and consistent training to consolidate it so that it is reliable and suitable for everyday use.
Step 1: Addressing and cue 🗣️
During the walk, we calmly address the dog by its name while walking.
After a short pause, we say “stand” calmly and slightly drawn out (pronounced: “staaaand”).
Step 2: Leash aid and hand support 🤝
At the same time, we slow the dog down slightly with gentle leash assistance.
Our hand calmly encircles the dog's waist from the outside towards the belly to prevent an involuntary sitting down – while we continue to say “stand” calmly.
Step 3: Withdrawing support and praise 🌟
As soon as the dog stands for a short time without support – so we have already taken the supporting hand away somewhat –, we address it by name and walk on a few steps with simultaneous praise.
Throughout the entire stand procedure, calm and praising confirmation is permitted.
Step 4: Correction when sitting down 🔄
If the dog wants to sit down, the correction consists of making a feigned step forward to get the dog to stand up.
Afterwards we proceed as described above – calm cue, gentle support, patient praise.
Step 5: Progress and withdrawing the aids 📈
Over the course of the weeks – provided the training is good – we will notice that our dog carries out the cue “stand” increasingly reliably and willingly.
As far as this progress goes, we can gradually withdraw the leash and hand support.
The calm, motivating communication with the dog is always maintained throughout.
The dog leaving the “stand” on its own should be corrected consistently but calmly.
Important notes ⚠️
Avoid harshly or sharply spoken commands in training and in everyday use – your dog might misinterpret a sharply spoken “stand” and sit or lie down instead.
Avoid “stand” in demanding or distraction-rich situations as long as the exercise is not yet consolidated.
Avoid stress during the entire stand procedure.
Avoid the dog leaving the “stand” position on its own without a release cue having been given.
Practical impulse: Daily routine

Use every walk as a training moment. Consciously choose quiet passages without distraction in which to include “stand”. Over time you will notice how your dog carries out the signal ever more joyfully and independently – a clear sign that your patient consistency is bearing fruit.
→ Did I make sure of a calm and distraction-free environment?
→ Did I carry out the training daily and repeatedly?
→ Did I address the dog calmly and attentively by its name?
→ Was the leash aid gentle and patient?
→ Was the support with the hand stress-free and fluid?
→ Did I make sure of calm communication with the dog?
→ Did I correct patiently and consistently?
→ Did I praise calmly and intensively?
